title: Research Bite #12: Optimizing Multiple-Choice Questions for Retrieval Practice
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #12 covers van den Broek and colleagues' study of “stepwise” multiple-choice questions, a format that displays the question stem alone for a few seconds — deliberately withholding the answer options — before revealing the choices, in order to prompt students to attempt cued recall from memory first. Across several experiments testing vocabulary learning, stepwise MCQs significantly outperformed standard MCQs (where question and options appear together) in most conditions. The benefit, however, is conditional: it is most robust when students actually try to recall the answer during that initial delay, and largely disappears for students who simply wait passively for the options to appear — meaning the format only works if students are explicitly told to use the gap for retrieval, not treat it as a pause. The researchers also confirm a separate, independent finding: competitive answer options (ones that can't easily be guessed or eliminated) produce better learning outcomes than weak distractors regardless of format, though the stepwise design offers a way to strengthen retrieval demand even when writing genuinely competitive distractors isn't feasible. Barton's classroom takeaway is a low-cost, easy-to-implement tweak: delaying the answer choices on a smartboard quiz or classroom-response system converts a recognition task into a small act of retrieval practice.
points: The stepwise format's core mechanism — a brief question-only delay before options appear — converts a passive recognition task into an act of active retrieval, directly linking it to the broader retrieval-practice literature covered elsewhere in the series.

The benefit is conditional on active use: students who simply wait for the options rather than attempting recall during the delay show little to no improvement, meaning the technique requires explicit instruction on how to use the pause, not just the pause itself.

Stepwise display is specifically flagged as valuable when writing genuinely competitive distractors isn't practical — it offers a route to stronger retrieval demand even with imperfect answer options.

Competitive answer choices (ones students can't easily guess or rule out) independently improve learning outcomes compared to weak distractors, reinforcing that MCQ quality is not just about the question but about how hard the wrong options make retrieval.

The format is explicitly framed as broadly deployable — computerized vocabulary exercises, classroom quizzes, mobile apps, smartboard practice, and lecture response systems are all named as viable settings — making it one of the more immediately actionable findings in the series.
quotes: This research article investigates the effectiveness of a novel multiple-choice question (MCQ) format—stepwise MCQs—for vocabulary learning. Stepwise MCQs present the question before the answer options, encouraging cued recall before revealing the choices.
Multiple experiments compared stepwise MCQs to standard MCQs, revealing that stepwise MCQs significantly enhanced vocabulary retention in most cases.

The benefits of stepwise MCQs are most robust when students actively try to recall the answer during the initial display of the question. Students who simply wait for the answer choices to appear do not show as much improvement.

Stepwise MCQs may be especially beneficial when it is not practical to create high-quality, competitive answer choices. Competitive answer choices require students to think carefully and rule out incorrect options.
Competitive answer choices, where students cannot easily guess the correct answer, lead to better learning outcomes than noncompetitive answer choices.
Overall, a stepwise display is a promising and easy-to-implement manipulation to optimize MCQs for retrieval practice
